cards.front: What three extra structures do plant cells have that animal cells do not have?
cards.answer: Chloroplasts / Permanent vacuole / Cell wall

cards.front: Why does a plant cell need a cell wall?
cards.answer: It strengthens and supports the cell, stopping it bursting when water enters by osmosis.

cards.front: What are the three stages of the cell cycle?
cards.answer: Growth and DNA replication / Mitosis / Division

cards.front: What four features make an exchange surface effective for diffusion?
cards.answer: Large surface area / Thin membrane (short diffusion path) / Rich blood supply / Ventilation

cards.front: Why do root hair cells need active transport to take up mineral ions from the soil?
cards.answer: Mineral ion concentration in the soil is often lower than in the root hair cell, so ions move against the gradient using energy from respiration.

cards.front: Why do some people object to embryonic stem cell research?
cards.answer: It involves destroying a human embryo, which they consider to be a potential human life.

cards.front: What are the three main groups of digestive enzymes?
cards.answer: Amylase / Protease / Lipase

cards.front: Amylase is produced in three places in the body. What are they?
cards.answer: Salivary glands / Pancreas / Small intestine

cards.front: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increase as temperature rises towards the optimum?
cards.answer: Molecules move faster and collide with the enzyme's active site more often, so the reaction happens more quickly.

cards.front: Why does the body need the amino acids absorbed from digested protein?
cards.answer: To build new proteins for growth and repair.

title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

cards.front: What are the four components of blood?
cards.answer: Plasma / Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets

cards.front: What are the three ways a red blood cell is adapted to transport oxygen?
cards.answer: Biconcave shape (larger surface area) / Packed with haemoglobin / No nucleus (more space for haemoglobin)

cards.front: Why is a double circulatory system more efficient than a single circulatory system?
cards.answer: Blood is pumped a second time after returning from the lungs, keeping pressure high so organs get oxygen quickly enough.

cards.front: Why are capillary walls only one cell thick?
cards.answer: It keeps the diffusion path short, so substances move quickly between the blood and surrounding tissues.

title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

cards.front: What are the five key plant tissues in a leaf and stem?
cards.answer: Epidermal tissue / Palisade mesophyll / Spongy mesophyll / Xylem / Phloem

cards.front: What four environmental factors increase the rate of transpiration?
cards.answer: Higher temperature / Lower humidity / More air movement (wind) / Higher light intensity

cards.front: Why does the epidermal tissue of a leaf produce a waxy cuticle?
cards.answer: To reduce water loss from the leaf surface.

cards.front: Why does higher temperature increase the rate of transpiration?
cards.answer: It increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, so more evaporate from the leaf surface.

cards.front: What are the four types of pathogen?
cards.answer: Bacteria / Viruses / Fungi / Protists

cards.front: What are the three ways white blood cells defend the body against pathogens?
cards.answer: Phagocytosis (engulfing pathogens) / Producing antibodies (target antigens) / Producing antitoxins (neutralise toxins)

cards.front: Why does an antibody only work against one particular pathogen?
cards.answer: It locks onto the unique antigens found only on that pathogen's surface.

cards.front: Why are most young children in the UK vaccinated against measles?
cards.answer: Measles can be fatal if complications arise, so vaccination protects against serious illness.

cards.front: What three measures reduce the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria?
cards.answer: Don't prescribe antibiotics inappropriately / Patients complete the full course / Restrict agricultural use of antibiotics

cards.front: What three things is a new drug tested for before it reaches patients?
cards.answer: Toxicity (is it safe?) / Efficacy (does it work?) / Dose (right amount)

cards.front: Why does herd immunity protect people who cannot be vaccinated themselves?
cards.answer: With most of the population immune, the pathogen cannot find enough hosts to spread to them.

cards.front: Why are very low doses of a new drug given first in clinical trials?
cards.answer: To check the drug is safe before testing it at higher doses.

cards.front: What are the three main factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis?
cards.answer: Light intensity / Carbon dioxide concentration / Temperature

cards.front: What are the five uses of the glucose made by photosynthesis?
cards.answer: Respiration (energy) / Storage as starch / Storage as fats and oils / Making cellulose / Making amino acids/proteins

cards.front: Why does increasing temperature increase the rate of photosynthesis, up to the optimum?
cards.answer: Molecules have more kinetic energy, so the reactions happen faster.

cards.front: Why does the body keep breathing heavily after vigorous exercise ends?
cards.answer: It needs extra oxygen to break down the lactic acid that built up in the muscles during anaerobic respiration.

cards.front: What are the five steps of aseptic technique when culturing bacteria, in order?
cards.answer: Sterilise equipment / Allow the loop to cool / Transfer the bacteria / Inoculate the agar plate / Seal and incubate

cards.front: What three ways can scientists confirm a diagnosis of plant disease?
cards.answer: Identification keys (dichotomous keys) / Testing kits (monoclonal antibodies) / Laboratory analysis (e.g. DNA testing)

cards.front: Why does nitrate deficiency cause stunted growth in a plant?
cards.answer: Nitrate ions are needed to make amino acids and proteins, without which the plant cannot grow properly.

cards.front: Why doesn't a large zone of inhibition mean an antibiotic works against all types of bacteria?
cards.answer: It may still be useless against a different species of bacteria not tested on that plate.

cards.front: Once a monoclonal antibody binds to a cancer cell, what three things can it do?
cards.answer: Trigger the immune system to attack the cell / Carry a toxic drug directly to the cell / Block signals that tell the cell to divide
items: Trigger the immune system to attack the cell
Carry a toxic drug directly to the cell
Block signals that tell the cell to divide

cards.front: What are the three main uses of monoclonal antibodies?
cards.answer: Pregnancy testing (detecting HCG) / Laboratory blood testing / Research (locating molecules)

cards.front: Why are transgenic mice with a human gene used to produce some monoclonal antibodies?
cards.answer: They produce human antibodies directly, avoiding the need to humanise mouse antibodies afterwards.

cards.front: Why did the TGN1412 trial raise questions about which volunteers should take part in drug trials?
cards.answer: The drug caused organ failure in six healthy volunteers, raising doubts about testing new drugs on people who are not already ill.

cards.front: What are the three essential components of every homeostatic control system?
cards.answer: Receptors / Coordination centres / Effectors

cards.front: What are the three types of neurone in the nervous pathway?
cards.answer: Sensory neurones / Relay neurones / Motor neurones

cards.front: Why are reflex actions faster than voluntary responses?
cards.answer: They do not involve the conscious brain — they are coordinated directly by the spinal cord.

title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control

cards.front: Which six glands make up the main endocrine system?
cards.answer: Pituitary gland / Thyroid gland / Adrenal glands / Pancreas / Ovaries / Testes

cards.front: Besides obesity, what four other factors increase the risk of Type 2 diabetes?
cards.answer: Sedentary lifestyle / Diet high in sugar and fat / Family history / Ethnicity
items: Diet high in sugar and fat

cards.front: Why is Type 1 diabetes not caused by lifestyle factors?
cards.answer: It's thought to be an autoimmune condition, where the immune system attacks the body's own insulin-producing pancreas cells.

cards.front: Why does the pituitary gland reduce TSH production as thyroxine levels rise?
cards.answer: Falling TSH means the thyroid makes less thyroxine, keeping thyroxine levels and metabolic rate stable.

cards.front: What are the four hormones that control the menstrual cycle?
cards.answer: FSH / LH / Oestrogen / Progesterone

cards.front: What are the four stages of the menstrual cycle, in order?
cards.answer: Menstruation (days 1-4) / Repair and build-up (days 4-14) / Ovulation (day 14) / Maintenance (days 14-28)

cards.front: Why does rising oestrogen stop more than one egg maturing in a cycle?
cards.answer: It inhibits further FSH release, so no more eggs are stimulated to mature that cycle.

cards.front: Why do fertility drugs (FSH and LH injections) carry a risk of multiple births?
cards.answer: They can cause multiple eggs to be released and fertilised at once, leading to twins or triplets.

cards.front: What four benefits does studying the human genome bring?
cards.answer: Find genes linked to disease / Develop personalised medicines / Trace human migration patterns / Compare how related species are

cards.front: What three parts make up a DNA nucleotide?
cards.answer: A sugar (deoxyribose) / A phosphate group / One of four bases

cards.front: Why is genetic variation among offspring important for a species?
cards.answer: It helps populations adapt to changing environments through natural selection.

cards.front: Why can DNA replicate itself accurately?
cards.answer: Each strand acts as a template, so a new complementary strand is built using fixed base-pairing rules.

cards.front: What are the three possible genotype combinations for a single gene?
cards.answer: Homozygous dominant (BB) / Heterozygous (Bb) / Homozygous recessive (bb)

cards.front: What four arguments are given in favour of embryo screening for inherited disorders?
cards.answer: Prevents serious, life-limiting conditions / Lets parents make informed choices / Reduces suffering for the family / May reduce harmful alleles over time
items: May reduce harmful alleles over time

cards.front: Why can a mother only ever pass on an X chromosome to her child?
cards.answer: She is XX, so every egg she produces carries an X chromosome.

cards.front: Why doesn't a 3:1 ratio guarantee that exactly 3 in 4 children will show the dominant trait?
cards.answer: Each child's genotype is an independent event, so the ratio is a probability, not a fixed outcome.

cards.front: What are the three main ways a fossil can form?
cards.answer: Mineralisation of hard parts / Casts or impressions in rock / Preservation in special conditions (ice, peat, amber)
items: Preservation in special conditions (ice, peat, amber)

cards.front: What five factors can cause a species to become extinct?
cards.answer: New predator / New disease / Increased competition / Environmental change / Catastrophic event

cards.front: Why are rare beneficial mutations important for evolution, even though most mutations have no effect?
cards.answer: They occasionally give an organism a survival advantage, and it is these mutations that drive evolutionary change.

cards.front: Why did the finches Darwin studied on the Galapagos Islands have different beak shapes?
cards.answer: Each beak shape was suited to a different food source available on that island.

cards.front: What are the six main abiotic factors that affect where organisms can live?
cards.answer: Light intensity / Temperature / Moisture level / Soil pH and mineral content / Wind speed and direction / Carbon dioxide levels

cards.front: What four biotic factors can affect a community?
cards.answer: Availability of food / New predators arriving / New pathogens / Competition for resources

cards.front: Why do camels have large flat feet and thick eyelashes?
cards.answer: Flat feet help them walk on sand, and thick eyelashes protect their eyes from sandstorms.

cards.front: Why do kangaroo rats produce very concentrated urine?
cards.answer: To conserve water in their desert environment.

cards.front: What four strategies help maintain biodiversity locally?
cards.answer: Breeding programmes / Seed banks / Protected areas / Hedgerow and habitat restoration

cards.front: What four types of government and global action help protect biodiversity?
cards.answer: Legislation (e.g. Wildlife and Countryside Act) / Recycling and waste reduction / Sustainable development / Global agreements (e.g. Paris Agreement)

cards.front: Why did introducing grey squirrels to the UK cause red squirrel numbers to decline?
cards.answer: Grey squirrels outcompete red squirrels for food and can carry squirrel pox, which harms red squirrels.

cards.front: Why is decomposition essential to the carbon cycle?
cards.answer: Without it, nutrients and carbon would stay locked in dead organisms and unavailable for new growth.

title: The Brain, the Eye and Temperature Control

cards.front: What are the six key parts of the eye, in the order light passes through them?
cards.answer: Cornea / Iris / Pupil / Lens / Retina / Optic nerve

cards.front: What three methods have scientists used to map brain regions to their functions?
cards.answer: Studying patients with brain damage / Electrically stimulating parts of the brain / MRI scanning
items: Electrically stimulating parts of the brain

cards.front: Why does a thin lens correctly focus light from a distant object?
cards.answer: It refracts light less, which suits the nearly parallel light rays coming from something far away.

cards.front: Why are the folds in the cerebral cortex important?
cards.answer: They increase its surface area, giving more space for neurones to carry out complex processing.

title: The Kidney, Water Balance and Plant Hormones

cards.front: What are the three main functions of the kidney?
cards.answer: Filtration of the blood / Selective reabsorption of useful substances / Excretion of waste as urine

cards.front: Gibberellins are involved in three plant processes. What are they?
cards.answer: Seed germination / Stem elongation / Flowering

cards.front: Why does dialysis fluid flow in the opposite direction to the blood in a dialysis machine?
cards.answer: It maintains a steep concentration gradient along the whole length of the membrane, so waste diffuses out efficiently.

cards.front: Why does a root bend downwards in response to gravity?
cards.answer: Auxin builds up on the lower side and inhibits cell elongation there, so the lower side grows more slowly and the root bends down.

title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom

cards.front: What four techniques can be used to separate mixtures?
cards.answer: Filtration / Simple distillation / Fractional distillation / Chromatography

cards.front: What are the three types of particle found inside an atom?
cards.answer: Protons / Neutrons / Electrons

cards.front: Why is the relative atomic mass of chlorine 35.5, not a whole number?
cards.answer: It's a weighted average of its two isotopes, chlorine-35 (75%) and chlorine-37 (25%).

cards.front: Why is most of the mass of an atom concentrated in the nucleus?
cards.answer: The nucleus contains the protons and neutrons, which have virtually all the mass; electrons have almost no mass.

title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups

cards.front: Compared to Group 1 metals, what three physical properties do transition metals have?
cards.answer: Higher melting points / Higher densities / Much stronger and harder

cards.front: What three key chemical properties do transition metals have?
cards.answer: Variable oxidation states / Form coloured compounds / Useful as catalysts

cards.front: Why do lithium, sodium and potassium all float on water?
cards.answer: They have low densities, lower than water.

cards.front: Why do melting and boiling points increase going down Group 7?
cards.answer: The molecules get larger, so the intermolecular forces between them become stronger.

cards.front: What are the three main types of chemical bonding?
cards.answer: Ionic bonding / Covalent bonding / Metallic bonding

cards.front: What three things must a dot and cross diagram for an ionic compound show?
cards.answer: Only outer shell electrons / Square brackets around each ion / The ion charge

cards.front: Why does a chlorine atom need to gain just one electron to become stable?
cards.answer: It already has seven electrons in its outer shell, so one more gives it a full shell of eight.

cards.front: Why do two nitrogen atoms form a triple covalent bond in a nitrogen molecule?
cards.answer: Each nitrogen atom needs three more electrons for a full outer shell, so they share three pairs.

cards.front: What are the four main types of structure in chemistry?
cards.answer: Giant ionic / Simple covalent (small molecules) / Giant covalent / Giant metallic

cards.front: What are the five changes of state between solid, liquid and gas?
cards.answer: Melting (solid to liquid) / Boiling (liquid to gas) / Freezing (liquid to solid) / Condensing (gas to liquid) / Sublimation (solid direct to gas)

cards.front: Why is diamond extremely hard?
cards.answer: Each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds in a rigid tetrahedral arrangement, so a huge network of bonds must be broken.

cards.front: Why is graphene an excellent conductor of electricity?
cards.answer: As a single layer of graphite, each carbon atom still has one delocalised electron free to carry charge.

title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations

cards.front: What are the four steps for calculating reacting masses from a balanced equation?
cards.answer: Write the balanced equation / Calculate moles of the known substance / Use the mole ratio for the other substance / Convert moles back to mass
items: Calculate moles of the known substance
Use the mole ratio for the other substance

cards.front: Why does relative formula mass (Mr) have no units?
cards.answer: It's a ratio compared with one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

cards.front: Why does adding more of the excess reactant make no difference to the amount of product formed?
cards.answer: The limiting reactant runs out first and determines how much product forms, regardless of the excess left over.

title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction

cards.front: Why must metals above carbon in the reactivity series be extracted by electrolysis rather than carbon reduction?
cards.answer: They are too reactive for carbon to displace them from their oxide, so electricity must be used instead.

cards.front: Why does potassium react far more vigorously than gold?
cards.answer: Potassium loses its single outer electron very easily, while gold holds onto its electrons tightly.

title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation

cards.front: What are the six steps for making a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt?
cards.answer: Warm the acid gently / Add the base until in excess / Filter to remove excess solid / Heat filtrate until crystals form / Leave to cool and crystallise / Pat the crystals dry
items: Add the base until in excess

cards.front: What three tools can be used to measure pH?
cards.answer: Litmus paper / Universal indicator / pH meter

cards.front: Why can a weak acid be concentrated but still chemically weak?
cards.answer: Concentration is how much acid is dissolved; strength is how much of it ionises — the two are independent.

cards.front: Why does the pH of an acid rise towards 7 during neutralisation?
cards.answer: Hydrogen ions from the acid react with hydroxide ions from the alkali to form water, removing H+ ions.

cards.front: What four types of ion are present when electrolysing an aqueous ionic solution?
cards.answer: The metal ion / The non-metal ion / H+ (from water) / OH- (from water)

cards.front: What three products are formed when brine (sodium chloride solution) is electrolysed?
cards.answer: Chlorine gas (at the anode) / Hydrogen gas (at the cathode) / Sodium hydroxide solution

cards.front: Why is recycling aluminium far cheaper than extracting new aluminium from bauxite?
cards.answer: New extraction needs a continuous, expensive electricity supply to keep the mixture molten and drive electrolysis; recycling avoids this.

cards.front: Why are electrodes in electrolysis usually made from inert materials like graphite or platinum?
cards.answer: So they do not react with the products being formed during electrolysis.

cards.front: What four types of reaction are examples of exothermic reactions?
cards.answer: Combustion / Neutralisation / Oxidation reactions / Hand warmers

cards.front: What four processes are examples of endothermic reactions?
cards.answer: Thermal decomposition / Dissolving citric acid and sodium hydrogen carbonate / Sports cold packs / Photosynthesis
items: Dissolving citric acid and sodium hydrogen carbonate

cards.front: Why is the reaction between hydrogen and chlorine exothermic?
cards.answer: More energy is released forming the new H-Cl bonds than is needed to break the H-H and Cl-Cl bonds.

cards.front: Why do instant cold packs keep the ammonium nitrate and water separated until use?
cards.answer: So the endothermic dissolving reaction only starts, absorbing heat, when the pack is needed and the barrier is broken.

cards.front: What are four uses of nanoparticles?
cards.answer: Sunscreens (UV protection) / Catalysts / Medicine (drug delivery) / Electronics and coatings

cards.front: What are the three particle size categories, from smallest to largest?
cards.answer: Nanoparticles (1-100 nm) / Fine particles (100-2500 nm) / Coarse particles (2500-10,000 nm)

cards.front: Why can nanoparticle catalysts reduce costs compared to using the bulk metal?
cards.answer: Their huge surface area provides many more active sites, so less material is needed to catalyse the same reaction.

cards.front: Why can nanoparticles pass through barriers such as the blood-brain barrier that larger particles cannot cross?
cards.answer: They are small enough to enter cells and pass through membranes that block larger particles.

title: Yield, Atom Economy, Molar Concentrations and Gas Volumes

cards.front: What three reasons explain why percentage yield is never 100% in practice?
cards.answer: The reaction may be reversible / Product is lost during transfer / Unexpected side reactions occur

cards.front: Why does an addition reaction always have an atom economy of 100%?
cards.answer: All the reactant atoms end up in the single product, with nothing wasted as a by-product.

cards.front: Why can a reaction have a high atom economy but still a low percentage yield?
cards.answer: Atom economy depends on the reaction's design, while percentage yield depends on how well it was carried out in practice.

title: Titrations, Chemical Cells and Fuel Cells

cards.front: What three advantages do hydrogen fuel cells have over combustion engines?
cards.answer: Only waste product is water / Don't run out while fuel is supplied / More efficient than combustion engines
items: Don't run out while fuel is supplied

cards.front: What four disadvantages do hydrogen fuel cells have?
cards.answer: Hydrogen is hard and costly to store/transport / Producing hydrogen often needs fossil fuels / Refuelling infrastructure is limited / Fuel cells are expensive to manufacture
items: Hydrogen is hard and costly to store/transport
Producing hydrogen often needs fossil fuels
Fuel cells are expensive to manufacture

cards.front: Why does a magnesium-copper cell produce a higher voltage than a zinc-copper cell?
cards.answer: Magnesium is much more reactive than zinc, and a bigger reactivity difference between the electrodes gives a higher voltage.

cards.front: Why is a rough titration carried out first, before the accurate titrations?
cards.answer: It gives an approximate volume, so later titrations can be run quickly until near the end point, then precisely.

title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory

cards.front: What are the four main factors that increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.answer: Temperature / Concentration / Surface area / Catalysts

cards.front: Why is the mass-loss method less accurate for reactions producing hydrogen gas?
cards.answer: Hydrogen is a very light gas, so the mass lost is too small to detect accurately.

cards.front: Why does the total volume of gas produced stay the same even when the acid concentration changes?
cards.answer: The same mass of marble chips is used each time, so the same amount of gas is eventually produced, just faster.

cards.front: What three conditions are used in the Haber process?
cards.answer: Compromise temperature (about 450C) / High pressure (about 200 atm) / Iron catalyst

cards.front: Why does increasing pressure favour ammonia production in the Haber process?
cards.answer: There are fewer moles of gas on the ammonia side (2 compared with 4), so raising pressure shifts equilibrium that way.

cards.front: Why isn't a low temperature used in the Haber process, even though it would give a better yield?
cards.answer: A low temperature would make the reaction too slow, so a compromise temperature is used instead.

cards.front: What are the six fractions produced by fractional distillation of crude oil, from top to bottom?
cards.answer: Gases / Petrol / Kerosene / Diesel / Fuel oil / Bitumen

cards.front: Why is carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion dangerous?
cards.answer: It binds to haemoglobin in the blood, preventing the blood from transporting oxygen.

cards.front: Why does bromine water decolourise when shaken with an alkene but not an alkane?
cards.answer: The bromine reacts with the alkene's carbon-carbon double bond, which an alkane does not have.

title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests

cards.front: What are the five steps of the paper chromatography method, in order?
cards.answer: Draw a pencil start line / Place spots of each substance on the line / Pour solvent below the line / Lower the paper into the solvent / Remove before the solvent front reaches the top
items: Place spots of each substance on the line
Lower the paper into the solvent
Remove before the solvent front reaches the top

cards.front: What four components make up a paint formulation?
cards.answer: Pigment (colour) / Solvent (keeps it liquid) / Binder (makes it stick) / Additives (control drying/finish)

cards.front: Why must the solvent level be below the pencil line in paper chromatography?
cards.answer: So the spots of substance don't dissolve directly into the solvent instead of moving up the paper.

cards.front: Why does seawater melt at a lower temperature than pure water?
cards.answer: The dissolved salt is an impurity, and impurities lower a substance's melting point.

title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect

cards.front: What three processes removed carbon dioxide from the Earth's early atmosphere?
cards.answer: Photosynthesis / Dissolving in the oceans / Formation of fossil fuels

cards.front: What four human activities are the main causes of rising atmospheric greenhouse gases?
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels / Deforestation / Agriculture / Landfill

cards.front: Why can water vapour amplify the greenhouse effect as temperatures rise?
cards.answer: Higher temperatures cause more water to evaporate, and water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas.

cards.front: Why does carbon capture and storage reduce a power station's carbon footprint?
cards.answer: It captures CO2 before it enters the atmosphere and stores it underground instead.

cards.front: What are the four main atmospheric pollutants produced by burning fossil fuels?
cards.answer: Carbon monoxide / Sulfur dioxide / Nitrogen oxides / Particulates

cards.front: What four methods can reduce atmospheric pollution from burning fuels?
cards.answer: Catalytic converters / Flue gas desulfurisation / Using cleaner fuels / Regular maintenance of engines/boilers

cards.front: Why does nitrogen oxide pollution lead to photochemical smog in cities?
cards.answer: In sunlight, nitrogen oxides react with other pollutants in the air to form smog.

cards.front: Why can particulates penetrate deep into the lungs and even the bloodstream?
cards.answer: They are so small that they can pass deep into the lungs and even across cell membranes.

cards.front: What are the four stages of a life cycle assessment?
cards.answer: Extracting raw materials / Manufacturing and processing / Use and distribution / Disposal

cards.front: What are the three Rs for reducing the environmental impact of products?
cards.answer: Reduce / Reuse / Recycle

cards.front: Why are phytomining and bioleaching more environmentally friendly than traditional mining?
cards.answer: They don't need huge amounts of energy and don't produce large volumes of waste rock.

cards.front: What three types of addition reaction can alkenes undergo?
cards.answer: Addition of hydrogen (hydrogenation) / Addition of water (hydration) / Addition of halogens

cards.front: What are the first four alcohols in the homologous series?
cards.answer: Methanol / Ethanol / Propanol / Butanol

cards.front: Why does fermentation have lower energy costs than making ethanol by hydration of ethene?
cards.answer: Fermentation happens at low temperatures (25-35C), while hydration needs high temperature and pressure (300C, 60-70 atm).

cards.front: Why does ethanoic acid have a higher pH than hydrochloric acid at the same concentration?
cards.answer: Ethanoic acid only partially ionises, so it produces fewer H+ ions than the fully-ionising hydrochloric acid.

cards.front: What are the three key naturally occurring polymers?
cards.answer: Proteins / Starch / DNA

cards.front: Why does an addition polymer have the same empirical formula as its monomer?
cards.answer: No atoms are lost or gained during addition polymerisation, unlike condensation which releases water.

cards.front: Why does producing water as a by-product identify a reaction as condensation polymerisation, not addition?
cards.answer: Addition polymerisation produces only the polymer; a water by-product means monomers reacted via their functional groups instead.

cards.front: What four advantages do instrumental methods like flame emission spectroscopy have over manual chemical tests?
cards.answer: Very sensitive (detects tiny amounts) / Fast and accurate / Can identify multiple elements at once / Needs only a small sample
items: Can identify multiple elements at once

cards.front: Why can aluminium hydroxide be distinguished from calcium and magnesium hydroxide, even though all three form white precipitates?
cards.answer: Aluminium hydroxide dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide is added, but calcium and magnesium hydroxide do not.

cards.front: Why is dilute hydrochloric acid added before barium chloride when testing for sulfate ions?
cards.answer: It removes any carbonate ions first, preventing them from giving a false positive white precipitate.

title: Materials, Corrosion, Haber Process and Fertilisers

cards.front: What are four barrier methods of preventing rust?
cards.answer: Painting / Oiling or greasing / Electroplating / Galvanising

cards.front: What are the three elements in NPK fertiliser?
cards.answer: Nitrogen (leaf and stem growth) / Phosphorus (root development) / Potassium (disease resistance, flowers/fruit)

cards.front: Why is reinforced concrete strong in both compression and tension, unlike plain concrete?
cards.answer: Steel bars embedded in the concrete add tensile strength that the cement matrix alone lacks.

cards.front: Why are unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen recycled in the Haber process?
cards.answer: Only about 15% converts to ammonia, so recycling the leftover gases improves overall efficiency.

title: DNA Structure, Cloning and the History of Genetics

cards.front: What are the four stages of speciation?
cards.answer: Geographical isolation separates populations / Different environmental conditions / Mutations create new alleles; natural selection acts differently / Populations can no longer interbreed
items: Mutations create new alleles; natural selection acts differently

cards.front: What three reasons explain why Mendel's ideas were ignored during his lifetime?
cards.answer: He worked in isolation, poorly connected / No known mechanism (genes/chromosomes undiscovered) / His mathematical approach was unusual for the time
items: He worked in isolation, poorly connected
His mathematical approach was unusual for the time

cards.front: Why can a mutation in a gene lead to a non-functioning protein?
cards.answer: It can change the triplet code, so a different amino acid is inserted and the protein may not fold or function correctly.

cards.front: Why does natural selection act differently on two geographically isolated populations of the same species?
cards.answer: They experience different environmental conditions, so different characteristics become advantageous in each population.

title: Trophic Levels and Transfer of Biomass

cards.front: What four ways is biomass lost between trophic levels?
cards.answer: Not all organisms are eaten / Not all parts are digested / Energy used in respiration/life processes / Excretory products (urea, CO2)

cards.front: Why are top predators always rare in an ecosystem?
cards.answer: Not enough energy and biomass reaches the top of the food chain to support large populations.

cards.front: Why can farming grazing animals still make sense, even though eating plants is more efficient?
cards.answer: Grazing animals can use land unsuitable for crops, and animal products provide nutrients plants can't.

cards.front: What are six threats to food security?
cards.answer: Rising birth rate / Changing diets (more meat) / New pests and pathogens / Environmental change (climate, drought, flooding) / Conflict and poverty / Cost of agricultural inputs

cards.front: What four strategies help make fishing sustainable?
cards.answer: Fishing quotas / Controlling net mesh size / Banning fishing in breeding season / Fish farming (aquaculture)

cards.front: Why does restricting an animal's movement and keeping it warm increase its growth rate in factory farming?
cards.answer: Less energy is lost through movement and maintaining body temperature, leaving more energy available for growth.

cards.front: Why could GM genes spreading into wild plants create a problem?
cards.answer: Cross-pollination can pass the modified gene into wild plants, which could then become very hard to control.

cards.front: What are the four energy transfer pathways?
cards.answer: Mechanically (by a force) / Electrically (by a current) / By heating / By radiation

cards.front: Why does doubling a spring's extension quadruple its elastic potential energy?
cards.answer: Extension is squared in the equation, so doubling it multiplies the stored energy by four.

cards.front: Why is no real energy transfer 100% efficient?
cards.answer: Some energy is always dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings.

title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources

cards.front: What are four types of thermal insulation used to reduce energy loss from a house?
cards.answer: Loft insulation / Cavity wall insulation / Double glazing / Draught excluders

cards.front: Why does insulation keep a flask of hot water hot for longer?
cards.answer: It prevents the thermal energy from transferring out to the surroundings.

title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference

cards.front: What three I-V graph shapes must you be able to recognise, and which component does each represent?
cards.answer: Straight line through origin: ohmic conductor / Curve that flattens: filament lamp / Current in one direction only: diode
items: Straight line through origin: ohmic conductor
Current in one direction only: diode

cards.front: Why does a thermistor's resistance decrease as its temperature rises?
cards.answer: The semiconductor material releases more charge carriers as it heats up, making it easier for current to flow.

cards.front: Why does an LDR's resistance decrease in bright light?
cards.answer: Photons of light release charge carriers in the semiconductor, so more light means lower resistance.

cards.front: What four properties are compared between series and parallel circuits?
cards.answer: Current / Voltage / Resistance / What happens if a component breaks
items: What happens if a component breaks

cards.front: Why does adding more resistors in series reduce the current flowing in the circuit?
cards.answer: It increases the total resistance, and higher resistance means less current flows for the same voltage.

cards.front: Why does adding more branches to a parallel circuit decrease its total resistance?
cards.answer: Each new branch gives current an additional path to flow through, so overall resistance drops.

title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid

cards.front: Why does even a small reduction in current cause a big drop in energy wasted as heat in cables?
cards.answer: Power loss depends on current squared (P=I2R), so reducing current has a squared effect on reducing the loss.

cards.front: Why is the live wire dangerous even when an appliance is switched off?
cards.answer: It can still carry a potential difference of about 230V relative to earth.

title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State

cards.front: What are the six changes of state?
cards.answer: Melting / Boiling / Evaporation / Condensation / Freezing / Sublimation

cards.front: What are the five steps for measuring the density of an irregular solid using a eureka can?
cards.answer: Measure the mass / Fill the eureka can until it overflows / Lower the object into the water / Read the displaced water volume / Calculate density using rho = m/V
items: Fill the eureka can until it overflows
Lower the object into the water

cards.front: Why does evaporation cause a liquid to cool down?
cards.answer: The fastest, most energetic particles escape first, lowering the average kinetic energy of those left behind.

cards.front: Why are gases much less dense than solids?
cards.answer: Gas particles are spread far apart, unlike the tightly packed particles in a solid.

title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat

cards.front: What are the five regions of a heating curve, in order?
cards.answer: Solid heating (temp rises) / Melting (temp constant) / Liquid heating (temp rises) / Boiling (temp constant) / Gas heating (temp rises)

cards.front: What four stages of calculation find the total energy to heat ice at -10C to steam at 100C?
cards.answer: Heat the ice to 0C / Melt the ice at 0C / Heat the water to 100C / Boil the water at 100C

cards.front: What are the three main types of nuclear radiation?
cards.answer: Alpha / Beta / Gamma

cards.front: What three precautions do workers take when handling radioactive materials?
cards.answer: Wear protective clothing / Use tongs to increase distance / Keep exposure time short

cards.front: Why is contamination generally more dangerous than irradiation?
cards.answer: You can't move away from radioactive material that is on or inside you, unlike an external irradiation source.

cards.front: What three practical uses does static electricity have?
cards.answer: Spray painting (and crop sprayers) / Photocopiers and laser printers / Electrostatic precipitators (removing soot/ash)

cards.front: Why does sparking occur when the potential difference between a charged object and earth is high enough?
cards.answer: The strong electric field ionises the air molecules, creating a conducting path for charge to flow through.

cards.front: When a sealed gas is heated, what three things happen that explain the rise in pressure?
cards.answer: Particles gain kinetic energy / Particles collide more frequently with the walls / Particles collide with greater force
items: Particles collide more frequently with the walls

title: Nuclear Radiation: Uses, Fission and Fusion

cards.front: What are the four main natural sources of background radiation?
cards.answer: Radon gas / Rocks and soil / Cosmic rays / Food and drink

cards.front: What four key components does a nuclear reactor contain?
cards.answer: Fuel rods / Control rods / Moderator / Coolant

cards.front: Why is technetium-99m's short half-life of about 6 hours useful for a medical tracer?
cards.answer: It does not stay radioactive inside the patient for long, minimising their radiation exposure.

cards.front: Why is beta radiation ideal for monitoring material thickness, rather than alpha or gamma?
cards.answer: Alpha would be stopped by any solid, while gamma passes through unaffected by small thickness changes.

cards.front: What are the five contact forces?
cards.answer: Friction / Air resistance / Tension / Normal contact force / Upthrust

cards.front: What are the three non-contact forces?
cards.answer: Gravitational force / Electrostatic force / Magnetic force

cards.front: Why does a boat float on water?
cards.answer: The upthrust from the water pushing up equals the boat's weight pushing down.

cards.front: Why does a person weigh less on the Moon than on Earth, despite having the same mass?
cards.answer: The Moon's gravitational field strength is weaker (about 1.6 N/kg vs Earth's 9.8 N/kg), and weight depends on g.

title: Work Done, Elasticity and Hooke's Law

cards.front: What are the steps of the force-extension required practical, in order?
cards.answer: Set up spring, clamp and ruler / Measure the spring's natural length / Add known weights one at a time / Measure the new length each time / Calculate extension = new length minus original length
items: Set up spring, clamp and ruler
Add known weights one at a time
Measure the new length each time
Calculate extension = new length minus original length

cards.front: Why does work done against friction cause a temperature rise?
cards.answer: Kinetic energy is transferred to the thermal energy stores of the surfaces in contact.

cards.front: Why is the energy transferred during inelastic deformation not fully recoverable?
cards.answer: Some of the energy is dissipated as heat rather than being stored elastically.

cards.front: Why is your displacement 0 m if you walk 3m north then 3m south, even though you travelled 6m?
cards.answer: Displacement only measures the straight-line distance from start to finish, and you ended up back where you started.

cards.front: What four criteria must be met for two forces to be a Newton's third law pair?
cards.answer: Same type of force / Equal in size / Opposite in direction / Act on two different objects

cards.front: What three everyday examples illustrate Newton's third law?
cards.answer: Walking / Rocket launch / Sitting on a chair

cards.front: Why does a full shopping trolley accelerate less than an empty one, when pushed with the same force?
cards.answer: It has more mass, and for a given force, greater mass produces smaller acceleration (Newton's second law).

cards.front: Why does a skydiver slow down after opening their parachute?
cards.answer: The parachute increases surface area, so drag force becomes greater than weight, decelerating the skydiver.

cards.front: What four factors increase a driver's thinking distance?
cards.answer: Tiredness / Alcohol and drugs / Distractions / Speed

cards.front: What four factors increase a vehicle's braking distance?
cards.answer: Wet or icy roads / Worn tyres or brakes / Higher speed / Greater mass

cards.front: Why does a tired driver react more slowly to a hazard?
cards.answer: Their nervous system processes signals less efficiently when tired.

cards.front: Why must the total momentum after an explosion still equal zero, even though fragments fly apart?
cards.answer: Momentum is conserved, so equal and opposite momenta of the fragments cancel out to zero overall.

cards.front: What are the four key properties used to describe any wave?
cards.answer: Amplitude / Wavelength / Frequency / Period

cards.front: What are four examples of transverse waves?
cards.answer: Light / Radio waves / Water surface ripples / S-waves (earthquakes)

cards.front: Why does measuring across several wavelengths give a more accurate result than measuring just one?
cards.answer: Any small measuring error is spread across many wavelengths, reducing the percentage error in each individual wavelength.

cards.front: What three medical/industrial uses do gamma rays have?
cards.answer: Sterilising instruments and food / Radiotherapy (treating cancer) / Medical tracers

cards.front: What three precautions do radiographers take to reduce X-ray exposure risk?
cards.answer: Stand behind lead-lined screens / Patients wear lead aprons / Keep exposure times short

cards.front: Why does a red shirt appear red?
cards.answer: It reflects red wavelengths of light and absorbs most of the other colours.

cards.front: Why are gamma rays more dangerous than radio waves?
cards.answer: Higher frequency waves carry more energy, and gamma rays have the highest frequency of all EM waves.

title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect

cards.front: What are four everyday uses of electromagnets?
cards.answer: Scrapyard cranes / Circuit breakers / Electric bells / Relays

cards.front: What are the four key components of a simple DC motor?
cards.answer: Rectangular coil of wire / Two permanent magnets / Split-ring commutator / Carbon brushes

cards.front: Why is an induced magnet always attracted to a permanent magnet, never repelled?
cards.answer: Its nearest pole always lines up opposite to the permanent magnet's pole, since opposite poles attract.

cards.front: Why can an electromagnet be used inside a circuit breaker to detect excessive current?
cards.answer: A stronger current makes a stronger magnetic field, which becomes strong enough to trip the switch and break the circuit.

title: Moments, Levers, Gears and Momentum Changes

cards.front: What three vehicle safety features work by increasing collision time?
cards.answer: Crumple zones / Seatbelts / Air bags

cards.front: What are four everyday examples of levers?
cards.answer: Crowbars / Wheelbarrows / Scissors / Spanners

cards.front: Why is it easier to open a door by pushing near the handle rather than near the hinge?
cards.answer: Pushing further from the hinge (pivot) creates a bigger moment for the same force.

cards.front: Why can a lorry and a bullet both have large momentum, despite very different masses?
cards.answer: Momentum depends on both mass and velocity, so the bullet's very high velocity compensates for its small mass.

title: Reflection, Sound Waves and Waves for Detection

cards.front: What three properties describe the image formed in a plane mirror?
cards.answer: Virtual (cannot be projected) / Upright (not upside down) / Laterally inverted (left-right swapped)

cards.front: What are the four internal layers of the Earth, discovered through seismic wave studies?
cards.answer: Crust / Mantle / Outer core (liquid) / Inner core (solid)

cards.front: Why do rough surfaces not produce a clear reflected image, even though each point obeys the law of reflection?
cards.answer: The surface is uneven, so reflected rays scatter in many directions instead of staying parallel.

cards.front: Why is the word 'AMBULANCE' written backwards on the front of an ambulance?
cards.answer: So it reads correctly when seen in a driver's rear-view mirror, since mirror images are laterally inverted.

title: Lenses, Visible Light and Black Body Radiation

cards.front: What are the three categories of material based on how they transmit light?
cards.answer: Transparent (transmits all light) / Translucent (transmits some, scatters it) / Opaque (transmits none)

cards.front: As a hot object like a star gets hotter, what five colours does it glow through in order?
cards.answer: Red / Orange / Yellow / White / Blue-white

cards.front: Why is a perfect black body also the best possible emitter of radiation?
cards.answer: A good absorber is also a good emitter, so absorbing all radiation makes it the best emitter too.

cards.front: Why does an object's temperature rise if it absorbs radiation faster than it emits it?
cards.answer: More energy is arriving than leaving, so the object's internal energy and temperature increase.

cards.front: What three factors increase the size of an induced potential difference?
cards.answer: Increasing speed of movement / Increasing magnetic field strength / Increasing number of coil turns

cards.front: What three core components do both a microphone and a loudspeaker contain?
cards.answer: A coil / A permanent magnet / A diaphragm or cone

cards.front: Why does the induced current direction stay the same if you reverse both the movement direction and the magnetic polarity together?
cards.answer: The two reversals cancel each other out, so the net effect on current direction is unchanged.

title: Space Physics: The Solar System and Beyond

cards.front: What are the four rocky (terrestrial) planets in our solar system, in order from the Sun?
cards.answer: Mercury / Venus / Earth / Mars

cards.front: What are the four gas giant planets in our solar system, in order from the Sun?
cards.answer: Jupiter / Saturn / Uranus / Neptune

cards.front: Why do we say space itself is expanding, rather than galaxies simply flying through space?
cards.answer: Every galaxy moves away from every other galaxy at once, like dots on an inflating balloon, showing space itself stretches.

cards.front: Why is cosmic microwave background radiation considered such strong evidence for the Big Bang?
cards.answer: No other theory can explain its existence as the leftover afterglow of the Big Bang.

title: Pressure in Fluids, Atmospheric Pressure and Upthrust

cards.front: What three factors affect the pressure at a given depth in a liquid?
cards.answer: Depth (height of the column) / Density of the liquid / Gravitational field strength

cards.front: Why is there no sudden edge where atmospheric pressure suddenly drops to zero?
cards.answer: The atmosphere has no clear boundary, it gradually thins out into space.

cards.front: Why is the force on the bottom face of a submerged cube greater than on the top face?
cards.answer: The bottom is deeper, so pressure there is higher; with equal face areas, that means a greater force.
